capability.title: More Than a Developer
capability.subtitle: Five disciplines most companies hire separately. I use them together, in sequence, on the same problem.
capability.note: These aren't five separate interests. **They're one loop.** Build something, get it found, measure what happens, connect it to the rest of the business, then use the evidence to decide what to improve next.

caseStudy.title: From a Website Problem to a
caseStudy.lede: An established service business needed to be found online. Following that problem honestly — all the way down the funnel — ended somewhere entirely different from where it started.

blocks.heading: The starting environment
paragraphs: Limited marketing infrastructure, limited existing assets, incomplete service information and no dedicated digital marketing function. Downstream sales and operational processes sat outside my direct authority.

blocks.heading: What I did
paragraphs: Built the website, then a dedicated service-page strategy targeting the specific commercial work the business wanted. Improved local SEO and the Google Business Profile. Added analytics and attribution so lead volume and source became measurable, then lead and call tracking on top of that.
Every stage was chosen by what the previous stage's data revealed — **not by a predefined scope.**

pivot.heading: The discovery
pivot.text: Once acquisition improved and better measurement was in place, call data exposed a major downstream lead-handling problem. **More traffic was no longer the only constraint.**
pivot.to: “What happens to the leads after we generate them?”

afterBlock.heading: Where that pushed the work
paragraphs: Attribution, CRM structure, call tracking, notifications, reminders, follow-up automation and pipeline thinking. The engagement stopped being a marketing project and became a revenue-operations one.

results: Google Search clicks grew from **40 to 90+ per rolling 28 days** between March and August 2026

process.title: Give Me the Problem, Not Just the Ticket
process.subtitle: The same six steps run whether the output is a website, a workflow, a report or a piece of software.

steps.title: Understand
steps.description: Learn how the business actually works — who buys, who sells, what breaks, who's involved and what everyone is already doing.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.description: Research the market, customer behaviour, the available data and the systems already in place, including the ones nobody documented.

steps.title: Identify
steps.description: Find the real constraint or opportunity — which is often not the thing that was originally asked for.

steps.title: Build
steps.description: Create the website, software, content, workflow or integration that addresses the constraint, at the smallest scope that will prove it out.

steps.title: Measure
steps.description: Instrument it and track what actually happened, not what was supposed to happen.

steps.title: Improve
steps.description: Use the evidence to find the next bottleneck, then start again one step further down the system.

process.note: I'm comfortable working from incomplete information. **Much of my strongest work has come from figuring out what needed to be done** rather than implementing predefined requirements.

background.title: I Understand the Business Behind the Software
paragraphs: I didn't learn business operations from a requirements document. **I've spent roughly 20 years around trades, construction, automotive, fleet, equipment and service businesses** — the people, machines, customers, schedules, estimates, delays, missed calls and real-world problems that software is supposed to help with.

That sits alongside modern web development, software, SEO, digital marketing, automation and AI. When a company describes an operational problem, I've usually seen the physical version of it, not just the ticket describing it.

real.heading: Real-world operations
real.body: 20 years around crews, equipment, estimates, dispatch, customers and the way work actually gets scheduled and won.

technical.heading: Technical systems
technical.body: Development, search, analytics, CRM, integrations, automation and AI workflows.

result.heading: The result
result.body: Solutions built for how the business runs — not just for how the spec was written.

projects.title: Four Projects, Four Different Proofs
projects.subtitle: Each one exists because a business problem needed something built. Problem, what I built, what it demonstrates.

cards.name: Service-Business Growth System
cards.role: Growth, SEO and lead-system build for a local excavation company
cards.problem: Effectively invisible for the commercial work the business wanted, with no way to tell where any lead came from.
cards.built: Website, targeted service pages, local SEO and Business Profile work, then analytics, attribution, call tracking and follow-up systems.
cards.proves: I can **own an outcome end to end** in an ambiguous environment and keep following the problem past my original scope.

cards.name: ALL8 Webworks
cards.role: Service-business lead-system platform and my own testing environment
cards.problem: Service businesses buy websites when what they actually lose is leads, somewhere between the search and the signed job.
cards.built: The positioning, the site, the conversion architecture, the SEO structure and the acquisition approach behind it.
cards.proves: **Commercial judgement** — I can define an offer, build the thing that sells it, and be accountable for whether it works.

cards.name: Estivor
cards.role: Trade-focused estimating and contractor workflow software
cards.problem: Contractors quote in spreadsheets and memory, then lose margin and follow-up between the estimate and the job.
cards.built: Next.js application, estimating and workflow architecture, CRM model, AI assistance and third-party integrations.
cards.proves: **Product thinking on real domain knowledge** — software designed around how contractors actually price and win work.

cards.name: ScoutChase
cards.role: AI-assisted prospecting and sales workflow tool
cards.problem: Prospecting eats the day: research, qualification and follow-up are manual, repetitive and easy to drop.
cards.built: AI-assisted research and qualification workflow, pipeline model, automation logic and a deliberately simple interface over it.
cards.proves: **I can apply AI to a real workflow** rather than bolt a chat box onto a product.
